strengths: The proposed method is simple, well-motivated, and practical: prepending a single Contextual token from a lightweight (110M) bidirectional encoder preserves the original causal attention architecture while giving every token access to contextual information, and concatenating the Contextual and EOS hidden states is a sensible pooling scheme that directly targets the recency bias of last-token pooling.

Experiments are broad and reasonably rigorous: the method is validated on three LLM backbones (1.3B–7B) across the full 56-dataset MTEB, with an explicit comparison protocol restricted to models trained on publicly available retrieval data, plus efficiency measurements (sequence length and inference time) showing large reductions (up to 85% length, 82% time) versus ECHO and bge-en-icl.

The ablation studies are thorough and genuinely informative: component-wise ablations (Table 2), number and position of Contextual tokens, frozen vs. trainable bidirectional encoder, alternative representation methods, and different encoder choices, with a meaningful MTEB-MINI subset construction and per-dataset results in the appendix.

Reproducibility support is strong: training data composition, per-dataset instructions, full hyperparameters (LoRA rank/alpha, batch sizes, steps), base model identifiers, and complete per-dataset MTEB results are provided; the method itself requires only standard components (E5-base-v2, LoRA, InfoNCE), making replication feasible.

The analysis adds useful empirical observations, e.g., that a single Contextual token suffices while multiple tokens degrade performance, and that the LLM-derived Contextual hidden state works better in the concatenation than the raw encoder output.
weaknesses: The headline SOTA claim (66.10 vs. 66.08 for bge-en-icl few-shot) is a 0.02-point margin with no statistical significance testing or multiple runs, and the improvements over LLM2Vec (0.78–1.30 average points) and over the own baseline with only the Contextual token (0.24–0.37 points on MTEB-MINI) are small and also reported without variance or significance estimates; single-run results on 56 datasets make these margins hard to interpret confidently.

The framing that gains stem from 'preserving pretraining semantics under causal attention' is somewhat confounded: the Contextual token is produced by E5-base-v2, itself a strong embedding model, so a substantial part of the signal is imported rather than unlocked from the LLM. The w/o Bi-Encoder ablation (61.74 vs. 62.63 for S-LLaMA-1.3B) suggests the marginal contribution of the mechanism itself is modest, and the paper's claim that improvements 'primarily stem from addressing causal attention and last-token pooling shortcomings' is not fully supported by this ablation.

The central theoretical claim about a pre-train/fine-tune attention mismatch compromising bidirectional adaptation is asserted but never directly demonstrated (no probing, analysis, or controlled experiment isolating the mismatch effect), leaving a key motivating argument as speculation.

The 'SOTA among models trained solely on publicly available retrieval data' comparison category is self-defined and excludes strong methods (e.g., NV-Embed with additional data, MGH) that would otherwise rank higher; ECHO results on LLaMA-2-7B are missing, weakening one of the direct comparisons.

Novelty is incremental: the core ingredients (a summary/pseudo token distilled from a smaller encoder, and concatenation-based pooling) resemble established techniques from multimodal adapters and prior pooling work, so the contribution is primarily an empirical demonstration rather than a new technique.

Minor presentation issues remain, e.g., a typo in the running example ('dog bits the jacket'), and the discussion of Table 6 contradicts the text slightly (text says 'better-performing bidirectional encoder (e.g., E5-base vs. E5-small)' while the table lists E5-small-v2 above E5-base-v2 with higher scores in some columns), which could confuse readers.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the method is tested on three decoder-only backbones (1.3B–7B) across the full 56-dataset MTEB, with per-dataset results, a well-motivated MTEB-MINI subset for ablations, and a large appendix with hyperparameters, training data, and instruction templates.

Extensive ablation studies covering component contributions, encoder freezing, token placement, number of Contextual tokens, and choice of bidirectional encoder (Tables 2–6, 10–12), plus an efficiency analysis (Figure 2) supporting the claimed sequence-length and latency reductions.

The method is architecturally simple and model-agnostic: it requires no changes to the LLM's attention mechanism, which is a practically attractive property compared to bidirectional-conversion approaches like LLM2Vec or NV-Embed.
The paper is generally well written and clearly structured, and the attempt to restrict comparisons to models trained only on public retrieval data is a reasonable effort at fairness.
weaknesses: The headline claims rest on very small margins. The 'state-of-the-art' result over bge-en-icl (few-shot) is 66.10 vs. 66.08 without ICL (essentially a tie), and 66.85 vs. 66.08 with ICL (+0.77). No statistical significance, variance, or seed analysis is reported anywhere, so these differences—on averages over 56 datasets—are difficult to distinguish from noise.

The novelty is incremental. Prepending a single soft token that summarizes the input is closely related to soft prompting, query/document augmentation, and the ICL-style context injection of bge-en-icl; concatenating two hidden states for pooling is a minor design choice. The paper does not adequately differentiate the mechanism from these prior ideas beyond the efficiency argument.

A central claim—that Causal2Vec's gains come from fixing causal attention's contextual-information deficit rather than from the bidirectional encoder's own embedding quality—is only weakly supported. The Contextual token is produced by E5-base-v2, itself a strong sentence embedder distilled on large contrastive data; Table 6 shows encoder quality strongly correlates with final performance. The 'attention mismatch compromises pretrained knowledge' argument is asserted repeatedly but never directly evidenced (e.g., no probing or controlled comparison isolating this effect).

Comparison fairness is incomplete. Several baselines' scores are quoted from prior papers rather than rerun under matched settings; ECHO has missing entries for S-LLaMA-1.3B in Table 1; and the efficiency claims in Figure 2 are based on only six selected MTEB subsets, so the 'up to 85%/82%' reductions are best-case numbers on very short datasets (Sprint., Emotion.), not representative averages.

Reproducibility is not adequately supported: no code, model weights, or training scripts are indicated as released, and no reproducibility statement appears in the manuscript. Given that the main contribution is empirical, this is a significant gap.

Some analysis is superficial or internally inconclusive: the recency-bias mitigation claim for concatenating Contextual and EOS states is contradicted in spirit by the paper's own L2-norm analysis (Figure 3, Appendix C.1), which shows the EOS token dominates the concatenated representation; explanations for Bi-LoRA effects (Section 4.5.2) and the Bi-EOS result (Appendix C.2) are speculative.

Given the combination of marginal gains, limited mechanistic insight, and lack of released artifacts, the contribution does not yet clearly exceed the threshold of a solid technical report over existing methods (ECHO, bge-en-icl, LLM2Vec) for main-conference consideration.

strengths: The proposed method is simple, well-motivated, and elegant: a single Contextual token from a lightweight bidirectional encoder restores access to contextualized information under causal attention without architectural modification, and concatenating Contextual and EOS hidden states is a sensible, low-cost pooling refinement.

Empirical evaluation is broad and disciplined: results across three LLM backbones (1.3B to 7B) on the full 56-dataset MTEB, with a deliberately fair comparison protocol restricted to models trained on public retrieval data, which credibly tests generalization to unseen non-retrieval tasks.

The ablation studies are thorough and genuinely informative: component ablations (Table 2), number of Contextual tokens (Table 5), choice of bidirectional encoder (Table 6), freezing vs. finetuning the encoder (Table 3), token position (Table 4), and alternative representation methods (Table 10) collectively substantiate the design choices rather than leaving them as ad-hoc decisions.

The efficiency analysis (Figure 2) quantifies a real practical advantage: up to 85% shorter sequences and 82% faster inference than bge-en-icl, and the finding that Causal2Vec-LLaMA-2-7B rivals Mistral-7B-based methods is a notable result.

Reproducibility support is good: hyperparameters, base model identifiers, training datasets with sample ratios, all instruction templates, and the MTEB-MINI composition are fully documented in the appendix, and a limitations section is included.
weaknesses: The headline SOTA claim is scoped narrowly ('models trained solely on publicly available retrieval datasets'). This exclusion criterion filters out many stronger systems (e.g., those using synthetic or proprietary data), so the practical significance of the top MTEB rank is limited and should be stated more carefully.

Reported improvements over the closest comparable baseline (LLM2Vec under identical training data) are modest (0.78 to 1.30 average points), and there is no evidence of run-to-run variance, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing, which is concerning given gains of similar magnitude are used to justify ablation conclusions (e.g., 0.13-0.29 point differences in Table 3).

The central argument that bidirectional attention causes a 'pre-train/fine-tune attention mismatch' that compromises pretrained semantic knowledge is asserted but never directly tested; the paper would benefit from targeted evidence (e.g., probing or comparing finetuned bidirectional vs. causal variants beyond aggregate MTEB scores).

The 'decoder-only' framing is somewhat undermined by dependence on an external bidirectional encoder (E5-base-v2); while the method preserves the LLM's causal attention, the overall system is a hybrid, and the paper could more explicitly acknowledge this, including the added deployment dependency.

The efficiency comparison in Figure 2 is restricted to a handful of selected MTEB subsets; inference-time claims would be more convincing with a systematic characterization across the full benchmark, including the encoder's own latency at scale.

No explicit statement of code/model release is provided; given the paper's positioning as a practical, adoptable technique, releasing artifacts would substantially strengthen reproducibility and impact.

Several ablation trends are small and explanations are speculative (e.g., why finetuning the bidirectional encoder helps the 1.3B model but hurts Mistral-7B), so some conclusions should be framed as hypotheses rather than findings.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and clearly presented: injecting a single Contextual token (produced by a lightweight bidirectional encoder) into the LLM input preserves causal attention while giving every token access to sentence-level context, and concatenating Contextual/EOS hidden states mitigates recency bias of last-token pooling.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the method is integrated into four backbones (1.3B–7B) and evaluated on all 56 English MTEB datasets, with comparisons against both bidirectional (LLM2Vec, GRITLM, NV-Embed, MGH) and causal (ECHO, bge-en-icl, Anchor, TP) methods under matched public training data and evaluation pipelines.

Extensive and genuinely useful ablations: number/placement of Contextual tokens, choice of bidirectional encoder, freezing vs. LoRA-tuning the encoder, alternative representation methods, noise-robustness of the pooling scheme, and embedding-concatenation baselines that rule out trivial fusion explanations.

Efficiency analysis (inference time and required sequence length) convincingly demonstrates the practical advantage over ECHO and bge-en-icl, and a compute-matched ICL variant strengthens the SOTA claim.
Good reproducibility support: fixed seed matching LLM2Vec, full hyperparameter tables, dataset composition, training/evaluation instructions, and GPU cost estimates are all provided.

The paper is candid about limitations (model scale, English-only, doubled embedding dimension) and includes a clear comparison of causal vs. bidirectional attention across backbones (Figure 3, Table 15).
weaknesses: The headline SOTA margin is very thin: 66.10 vs. 66.08 (bge-en-icl) and 66.10 vs. 65.87 (MGH) — differences of 0.02–0.23 points on MTEB with no significance testing, variance over seeds, or confidence intervals, so the 'new state-of-the-art' claim is fragile and the ablation gains (e.g., 0.38–0.60 from the Contextual token alone) are also small.

The method depends on an additional pretrained bidirectional encoder (E5-base-v2), which weakens the framing that gains come from 'preserving the LLM's causal attention': the baseline without the bi-encoder drops 1–2 points, so part of the improvement is effectively injecting an external embedding model's knowledge rather than unlocking latent capability of the LLM alone.

The central 'attention mismatch' hypothesis is supported only by aggregate performance comparisons (Figure 3, Table 15); there is no direct mechanistic evidence, and the Mistral-7B exception is explained away post-hoc via 'non-standard pre-training'.

Evaluation is limited to English MTEB and models up to 7B; MTEB is also known to have saturation/leakage concerns, and no complementary retrieval-only evaluation (e.g., BEIR) or multilingual results are provided.

No explicit statement that code or model checkpoints will be released, which matters for verification given the close margins and many design choices (placeholder tokens, encoder LoRA policies differing by model size).

The contribution is somewhat incremental: it combines known ingredients (soft-prefix/context tokens from an auxiliary encoder, per-layer or input-level contextual injection as in TP/PrefixTuning-style work) into a new configuration, so novelty rests mainly on the empirical finding rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

strengths: The proposed method is simple, architecture-preserving, and clearly motivated: injecting a single Contextual token distilled by a lightweight bidirectional encoder is a low-overhead alternative to bidirectional attention conversion or input duplication (ECHO, bge-en-icl).

The experimental coverage is broad: four LLM backbones (1.3B–7B), full MTEB (56 datasets) with per-dataset results in appendices, a compute-matched ICL variant, and an unusually thorough set of ablations (number/placement of Contextual tokens, choice of bidirectional encoder, representation methods, LoRA on the encoder, causal-vs-bidirectional within their own framework, noise robustness).

Efficiency analysis (inference time, required sequence length, embedding dimension/storage) is conducted and reported, directly supporting the 'low computational overhead' claim rather than leaving it asserted.

Reproducibility artifacts are reasonably complete: hyperparameters, LoRA configurations, exact HuggingFace checkpoints, training data curation, and evaluation instructions are documented, and the method builds on an openly available training set from Springer et al. (2025).
weaknesses: The headline SOTA claim rests on very thin margins: 66.10 vs. 65.87 (MGH) and 66.08 (bge-en-icl), and 66.85 vs. 66.08 for the ICL variant. With a single fixed seed per configuration and no variance estimates, significance tests, or multiple runs, these differences are well within plausible noise, and 'new state-of-the-art' is overstated.

The central narrative is confounded. The paper argues that preserving causal attention avoids a pre-train/fine-tune 'attention mismatch,' but the contextual information itself is produced by a full bidirectional E5 encoder at inference time. Causal2Vec is thus effectively an LLM-plus-bidirectional-encoder ensemble; the comparison against purely bidirectional LLM methods does not cleanly isolate the claimed benefit of retaining causal attention. The 'attention mismatch' explanation remains a hypothesis supported mainly by Figure 3 rather than by mechanistic analysis.

MTEB-MINI is self-curated ('empirically introduced') by the authors, and all ablations are run on it. Without evidence that the 30-dataset subset was fixed before tuning (e.g., pre-registration or held-out selection), there is a risk of incidental test-set selection bias, which matters given that many reported ablation deltas are 0.2–0.6 points.

Novelty is limited: the idea of prepending a compressed or summary vector to a causal LLM is closely related to prior token-prepending/pseudo-token approaches (TP, prompt/prefix methods, embedding-compression work). The paper positions itself against these only partially, and the strongest individual contributions (concatenation pooling, recency-bias mitigation) are incremental.

Several citations appear unverifiable or implausible (e.g., Jiang et al. 2026 arXiv:2604.10937; Zhang et al. 2026a,b arXiv:2601.02993 and a Web Conference 2026 page range), which undermines trust in the related-work claims and must be corrected and verified.

Writing and presentation issues reduce clarity: typos ('Contenation', 'Additiaonl', 'beg-en-icl', 'fint-tune'), a Figure 2 that is hard to parse, and some claims that contradict the fine print (e.g., 'adds no computational burden' while a 110M encoder must be run on every input; the retrieval-n robustness gap of 1.55–2.17 points is modest relative to the framing).

The scope restriction to models trained solely on public retrieval data is defensible but softens the practical significance: the comparison set is a narrow band of academic models, and the 0.02-point margin over bge-en-icl does not establish a meaningful practical advance.
No code release is explicitly promised, which, combined with seed sensitivity of sub-point differences, makes independent verification of the SOTA claim difficult.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and elegant: distilling contextual information into a single Contextual token via a lightweight bidirectional encoder and prepending it under the original causal mask sidesteps both the pre-train/fine-tune attention mismatch of bidirectional conversion and the extra-input cost of ECHO/bge-en-icl.

Empirical evaluation is comprehensive and convincing within its stated scope: four LLM backbones (1.3B–7B), full 56-dataset MTEB evaluation, and comparisons against strong bidirectional (LLM2Vec, GRITLM, MGH, NV-Embed) and causal (ECHO, Anchor, bge-en-icl) baselines under matched training data and pipelines.

The ablation suite is unusually thorough: component ablations (Table 2), direct embedding-concatenation control (Table 4), number of Contextual tokens (Table 5), choice of bidirectional encoder (Table 6), noise-robustness analysis of recency bias (Table 3), token position (Table 14), alternative pooling schemes (Table 12), and application to an existing strong embedder (e5-mistral-7b-instruct, Table 11). Appendix C.6 (causal vs. bidirectional within the same method) is a particularly nice controlled experiment supporting the central claim.

The efficiency analysis (Figure 4, Figure 6, Tables 13) substantiates the compute advantage claims with concrete measurements (up to 82% inference-time reduction vs. bge-en-icl, up to 85% shorter sequences vs. ECHO/ICL), showing the efficiency gains are real, not just architectural arguments.

Reproducibility support is above average: fixed seeds, complete hyperparameters (Table 7), explicit model checkpoints from HuggingFace, instruction templates for all datasets (Tables 8, 16), and full per-dataset results (Tables 17–18). The framing of comparisons restricted to models trained solely on public retrieval data is a fair and clearly stated scope.
The limitations section is honest and specific (scale, English-only, doubled embedding dimension, single-token sufficiency).
weaknesses: The novelty is modest. The method combines well-known ingredients — soft/contextual prompt tokens distilled from an auxiliary encoder, prepended conditioning tokens, and multi-vector concatenation pooling — so the contribution is primarily an empirical finding that this combination works well for causal-LLM embeddings rather than a new technique or insight.

The headline 'SOTA' claim is fragile: 66.10 vs. 66.08 over bge-en-icl, and even the ICL-augmented 66.85, are very small margins on a single benchmark with no statistical significance testing, variance over seeds, or error analysis. Given LoRA-only fine-tuning and evaluation noise on MTEB, these differences may not be meaningful, which weakens the strongest claim in the abstract.

The central narrative ('preserve causal attention, no bidirectional encoder needed') is somewhat overstated: the method still depends on an off-the-shelf bidirectional encoder (E5-base-v2) at both training and inference time to produce the Contextual token, so bidirectional contextualization is outsourced rather than eliminated; a two-stage inference pipeline is also introduced as a practical complication. This dependence deserves more candid framing.

Several ablation gains are small (e.g., CtxToken alone adds only 0.38/0.60 points in Table 2), and the paper's causal interpretations (e.g., why E5-large-v2 does not help, why Bi-LoRA helps small but hurts large models) remain speculative without deeper analysis.

Writing quality issues: multiple typos ('Additiaonl', 'Contenation', 'fint-tune', 'beg-en-icl'), and the references contain several implausibly future-dated entries (e.g., Jiang et al. 2026, arXiv:2604.10937; Zhang et al. 2026a,b), which undermines confidence in citation hygiene.

Evaluation is restricted to English MTEB and models under 7B parameters; no multilingual or long-context (beyond 512 tokens) evaluation limits the generality of the claims, and no code release is explicitly stated despite otherwise good reproducibility detail.
